findings.what: -sendChecks bails out on `if (!self.peerPwd.length || self.socketHandle < 0) return;`, but in reflector (transport) mode -start returns at line 38 before any socket is created, so _socketHandle stays -1 forever and the `if (self.transport) { self.transport(request); return; }` branch at lines 101-104 is unreachable dead code.
findings.failure: Every real call on this build uses the reflector transport (TGCall.mm:184 sets ice.transport). The 0.3s checker timer fires, hits the socketHandle guard and returns, so the client never emits a single STUN binding request. Only the peer's inbound checks are answered; our side never nominates a pair, the peer's ICE agent never sees a check from us, and the call sits in TGCallStateConnecting until the peer discards it.
findings.fix: In -sendChecks change the guard to `if (!self.peerPwd.length) return; if (!self.transport && self.socketHandle < 0) return;` so the transport branch at line 101 is reached. The socket guard must apply only to the direct-socket path below line 106.

findings.what: -teardown clears ice/reflectors/controller but never resets the signalling state it set up: `sentCandidates`, `callKey`, `signallingSeq`, `currentSenderTag`, `currentReflector`, `peerUfrag`, `peerPwd`, `localUfrag`, `localPwd`, `reflectorHost`. `sentCandidates` is a one-way latch, and -sendOurCandidates starts with `if (self.sentCandidates || !self.reflectorHost.length) return;` (line 173).
findings.failure: TGCall is a process-wide singleton (+shared). The first call sets sentCandidates=YES. Every subsequent call in the same app run reaches -probeReflectorsIn:key: -> -sendOurCandidates, returns immediately, and so never creates a TGCallIce, never sends its candidates message and never learns the peer's ufrag/pwd. The second and all later calls hang in Connecting and are discarded. Stale callKey also means signalling from the new call is decrypted with the old key until callStateReady arrives.
findings.fix: At the top of -teardown add: `self.sentCandidates = NO; self.callKey = nil; self.signallingSeq = 0; self.currentSenderTag = 0; self.currentReflector = nil; self.peerUfrag = nil; self.peerPwd = nil; self.localUfrag = nil; self.localPwd = nil; self.reflectorHost = nil; self.reflectorPort = 0;` (before the ice/reflector cleanup).

findings.what: Bounds checks in +parseCandidates use unchecked addition on 32-bit types: `uint32_t size = TGReadU32(bytes + at); at += 4; if (at + size > length) return nil;` (lines 120-123, repeated at 137-140). NSUInteger is 32 bits on armv7, so `at + size` wraps.
findings.failure: A candidates message whose length prefix is e.g. 0xFFFFFFF0 makes `at + size` wrap to a small value, the guard passes, and `[[NSString alloc] initWithBytes:bytes + at length:size ...]` reads ~4GB past the decrypted buffer -> EXC_BAD_ACCESS as soon as it walks off the page. The same happens on the ufrag/pwd loop. The body is peer-controlled (only the call key gates it), so any malformed or truncated candidates message from a modern tgcalls peer kills the app mid-call.
findings.fix: Replace both checks with subtraction that cannot overflow: `if (size > length - at) return nil;` (and `break;` in the credentials loop), keeping the preceding `if (at + 4 > length)` guards rewritten the same way as `if (length < 4 || at > length - 4)`.

findings.what: +wavFromOpusFile: decodes the entire voice note into an in-RAM NSMutableData with `op_read_stereo` at 48 kHz stereo (`const int channels = 2;`, line 39), then builds a second full copy: `NSMutableData *wav = [NSMutableData dataWithBytes:header length:44]; [wav appendData:pcm];` (lines 80-81) before writing it out.
findings.failure: Telegram voice notes are mono. A 60-second note becomes 48000*2*2*60 = 11.5 MB of PCM, plus NSMutableData's doubling reallocs (transient ~23 MB), plus the 11.5 MB `wav` copy, plus the atomic file write buffer: a 30-40 MB peak on a device with 40-60 MB usable. On the 4S, playing a two-minute voice note from a loaded chat screen is a jetsam kill, not a slow decode.
findings.fix: Write the WAV incrementally: open the output with NSFileHandle, write a 44-byte placeholder header, decode with `op_read` (mono, channels = 1) into the stack buffer and `writeData:` each block, then seek to offsets 4 and 40 and patch the RIFF/data sizes. Drop the `pcm` NSMutableData and the `wav` copy entirely; peak RAM becomes the 23 KB stack buffer.

findings.what: -stopRecording has an else branch that ends the recording without ever notifying anyone: `if (self.movieOutput.isRecording) [self.movieOutput stopRecording]; else self.recording = NO;`. -startRecording sets `self.recording = YES` (line 362) synchronously, but AVCaptureMovieFileOutput.isRecording only becomes YES once the output actually starts.
findings.failure: Tap-and-immediately-release the shutter (or an app-background event arriving in the same runloop turn as startRecording): stopRecording sees isRecording == NO, sets recording = NO and returns. -captureOutput:didFinishRecordingToOutputFileAtURL: never fires, so neither videoRecorder:didFinishRecordingToPath:... nor videoRecorder:didFailWithError: reaches TGVideoCaptureViewController - the capture screen stays in its recording UI forever. Worse, the movie output then does start and keeps writing to disk until the 10-minute / 64 MB limit, with nothing left holding the flag that would stop it.
findings.fix: Replace the else branch with a real termination: `else { self.recording = NO; self.discarding ? [self discardOutputFile] : [self failWithCode:TGVideoRecorderErrorTooShort]; self.discarding = NO; }` - or better, keep a `stopRequested` flag and call -stopRecording again from -captureOutput:didStartRecordingToOutputFileAtURL: so the pending stop is honoured once the output is really running.

findings.what: callStateReady is read straight out of the TDLib dictionary with no type guards: `NSData *key = [[NSData alloc] initWithBase64EncodedString:state[@"encryption_key"] options:0];`, and the same for `type[@"peer_tag"]` (line 451, 518) and `server[@"ip_address"]` (line 521).
findings.failure: If encryption_key is absent or is not a string (any TDLib schema drift, or a reply this build's schema does not match), -initWithBase64EncodedString:options: is handed nil/an NSNumber and raises NSInvalidArgumentException on iOS 6 - an uncaught crash on the main queue the moment a call reaches Ready. TGCallReflector -initWithHost: with a non-NSString host later crashes in -UTF8String at TGCallReflector.m:59.
findings.fix: Before line 433 add `NSString *encoded = [state[@"encryption_key"] isKindOfClass:NSString.class] ? state[@"encryption_key"] : nil; if (!encoded) { self.state = TGCallStateFailed; return; }` and use `encoded`. Guard `type[@"peer_tag"]` and `server[@"ip_address"]` with the same isKindOfClass:NSString.class check, skipping the server when either fails.

findings.what: -inspectReflectorPacket: dereferences the first four bytes with no length check: `if (packet.length <= 32){ NSLog(@"... first %02x%02x%02x%02x", ..., bytes[0], bytes[1], bytes[2], bytes[3]); return; }`. The only guard above it is that the packet is <= 32 bytes.
findings.failure: TGCallReflector -readLoop (TGCallReflector.m:164-181) forwards every datagram with `got > 0`, including 1-3 byte packets. A short/garbage UDP datagram from the reflector (or any host that guesses the ephemeral port) reads up to 3 bytes past the NSData allocation; on a page boundary that is an EXC_BAD_ACCESS during an active call.
findings.fix: Change the guard to `if (packet.length < 4){ NSLog(@"TGCall: %lu-byte reflector packet", (unsigned long)packet.length); return; } if (packet.length <= 32){ ...existing log... }`.

findings.what: -sendMedia: and the `onMedia` block property are never used anywhere in the tree: `onMedia` is only ever read at TGCallIce.m:151 and 176 and is never assigned (TGCall.mm sets only `transport` and `onConnected`), and -sendMedia: has no callers. TGCallMessages.h:16-17 `TGCallMessageMediaState`/`TGCallMessageAudioData` are declared and defined but never referenced either.
findings.failure: No runtime failure - but the media path looks wired up when reading TGCallIce.h, which is how the reflector-mode ICE work above got left half-finished. Anyone tracing why no audio flows will follow onMedia and find nothing on the other end.
findings.fix: Either delete -sendMedia:, the `onMedia` property and its two call sites plus the two unused message-type constants, or wire onMedia in TGCall.mm -sendOurCandidates alongside `transport`/`onConnected` and feed it into the audio path. Do not leave it declared and unassigned.

findings.what: Three private properties are written but never read: `reflectorPort` (written at line 538), `reflectorId` (written at line 539, and its value comes from the already-incremented `index` inside the NSLog on line 532), and `loggedHeader` (declared line 124, never written or read at all).
findings.failure: No runtime failure; each is 4-8 bytes of a singleton. They are leftovers from an earlier single-reflector design and make -probeReflectorsIn:key: look like it maintains state that later code depends on.
findings.fix: Delete the three @property lines (120, 121, 124) and the two assignments at lines 538-539.

findings.what: The decoded WAV always lands on one fixed path: `NSString *out = [NSTemporaryDirectory() stringByAppendingPathComponent:@"voice.wav"];`, unlike TGVoiceRecorder which uses a timestamp+random name (TGVoiceRecorder.m:33-37).
findings.failure: Decoding runs on a global queue (TGChatViewController.m:3928). Tap voice note A, then B before A's AVAudioPlayer has been created: B's decode overwrites voice.wav, and the main-queue block for A then builds its player from B's file - the user hears the wrong voice note. The file also never gets deleted, so temp holds one stale multi-MB WAV indefinitely.
findings.fix: Name the output after the source, e.g. `[NSString stringWithFormat:@"voice-%@.wav", opusPath.lastPathComponent]`, and have TGChatViewController remove the previous WAV in -stopPlayback.
